A flagpole is centered along a building at one of these locations in a photograph where the U.S. flag blows above the mountain tops in the background. The (*) identical houses in that photograph appear in the background of a baseball game photo taken for a photo-essay collection that includes photos of Toyo Miyatake's family and nurse Catherine Natsuko Yamaguchi. Ansel Adams and Dorothea Lange photographed, for 10 points, what facilities, such as Manzanar, used by the U.S. during World War II to incarcerate certain Asian Americans.
2.r: Japanese internment camps [accept Japanese camps; accept Japanese-American Relocation Centers accept reasonable equivalents of the places where Japanese-Americans were relocated during World War II; prompt on partial answers that only mention some sort of camp or holding facility; accept Manzanar internment camp or Manzanar relocation center before mentioned ]

2.q: A photographer for this magazine spent 6 years traveling to remote locations like the Republic of Dahomey to create a series of ethnographic holiday photos like "Christmas at Cuzco." While employed by this magazine, that photographer of "Still Life with Ace of Hearts" created a black and white portrait of Igor Stravinsky dramatically wedged into a corner. Irving Penn was a longtime photographer for this magazine, which in the 1940's commissioned Lee Miller's iconic photograph in Hitler's (*) bathtub. More recently, this magazine provoked controversy for a cover where Lebron James and Gisele Bundchen stand in a pose reminiscent of King Kong. For 10 points, name this fashion magazine edited since 1988 by Anna Wintour.

One artist from this present-day country included formalist photographs of objects like shoe irons and blast furnaces in his book The World is Beautiful. A very large photograph from this present-day country depicting a river flowing between two green fields under an overcast sky sold at Christie's for $4.3 million in 2011. A performance artist in this country planted 7000 oaks and locked himself in a room with a coyote. This home of Andreas Gursky and (*) Joseph Beuys has a Norman Foster-designed glass dome on its parliament building. Albert Renger-Patzsch and George Grosz belonged to this country's New Objectivity movement. Architects from this country designed the White City of Tel Aviv in the style of a school in this country founded by Walter Gropius, the Bauhaus. For 10 points, name this country home to the Reichstag.

James Franco was accused of appropriation when he placed himself in twenty-nine works in this medium displayed at the Pace Gallery in 2014. The works Bus With Reflections of Flatiron Building and Telephone Booths attempt to capture the effect of this medium, which inspired the work of an artist who strapped a paintbrush to his hand after becoming quadriplegic. "Hyperrealist" artists who imitate this medium include (*) Richard Estes and Chuck Close. An artist who works in this medium captured herself in stereotypical female roles in Untitled Film Stills. A Frenchman who wrote The Decisive Moment named Henri Cartier-Bresson pioneered the use of this medium in journalism. For 10 points, identify this art form used by Cindy Sherman and Alfred Stieglitz.

A photographer from this country created a diptych depicting four women striking the same poses in trench coats on the left and nude on the right. Husband and wife photographers from this country depicted industrial structures in Anonymous Sculptures. The first SUMO book of photography is by an artist from this country, with one of his Big Nudes on the cover. American artist Lee Miller was photographed in a leader of this country's (*) bathtub. A photograph from this country depicting a river flowing between two green fields is the most expensive ever sold. Yevgeny Khaldei took a photograph of a flag raised over a building in this country after a World War II battle. For 10 points, Andreas Gursky was from what country home to the Dusseldorf School?
2.r: Germany [or Deutschland; accept Federal Republic of Germany or answers like Nazi Germany etc.] (The husband and wife duo are Bernd and Hilla Becher; the photograph of a river described is Rhein II by Gursky.)

2.q: A man in this city is seen admiring a voyeuristic painting while window shopping with his wife in the photograph Sidelong Glance. The graffiti and nightlife of this city were documented by a Hungarian immigrant who was dubbed its "Eye," Brassai ("brah-SY"). Two actors staged an impromptu passionate embrace for a photo taken in this city titled Kiss By the City Hall. Near a (*) train station in this city, an artist captured a man jumping from a ladder into a shallow pool of water, illustrating the "decisive moment" he sought while photographing its streets. Early photographers who worked in this city include Nadar and the inventor of the daguerreotype ("da-GAIR-oh-type"). For 10 points, name this European capital, where many photos are taken of a thousand-foot-tall tower built by Gustav Eiffel.

"Sidney Allen" was the pseudonym used by Sadakichi Hartmann while writing critiques in one of this photographer's journals. This photographer commented that he had "photographed god" with regards to a picture he took at Lake George. A "round straw hat; funnel leaning left" inspired a picture by this photographer of the Equivalents series. Edward Steichen designed the cover for this photographer's journal (*) Camera Work. Sculptures by Constantin Brancusi (brahn-KOOSH) were among the avant-garde works exhibited at his 291 gallery. A woman holds a baby in front of a clothesline in this photographer's most famous work, which depicts crowded passengers on the SS Kaiser Wilhelm II. For 10 points, name this "godfather of modern photography," who took the photograph The Steerage.

This artist depicted the face and furs of a turbaned woman with round earrings larger than her eyes in Woman with a Veil on Fifth Avenue. Germaine Greer accused this artist of "kneeling astride [her]" and trying to distress her to uproot the image of the "sexy feminist that men like." This artist's works were unusually square in format. Another work by this artist inspired the corduroy-wearing girls in (*) Stanley Kubrick's The Shining. This photographer of Identical Twins [from] Roselle, New Jersey showed a suspender strap hanging down the arm of a boy with a rictus smile and clawed hands in Central Park; that boy holds a fake "Mk 2 Pineapple" weapon. For 10 points, name this photographer of "Child with Toy Hand Grenade" known for depicting transvestites, giants, and other marginalized figures.
2.c: 2015 STIMPY Pkt 10. Virginia A - Kentucky A Q4

2.q: An artwork in this medium features a model of a church organ sitting next to a statue of Jupiter Tonans and is named after Kynzvart Castle. A person getting their shoe shined can be seen at the bottom-left of a work in this medium that depicts the Boulevard du Temple. After secretly showing works in this medium to Francois Arago, their creator got into a (*) patent battle with Henry Fox Talbot, who had developed a rival process that used "salted paper." This medium's creator previously worked with Nicephore Niepce on the Heliograph. Works in this medium were created by blowing mercury vapor onto a silver-coated copper plate and then dipping it into a salt bath. For 10 points, give this medium, named after a French pioneer of photography.

A book of photographs depicting these people was criticized by Raymond Solokov in a Wall Street Journal article that placed black bars over a photo of one of them. The books Aperture and Still Time include photos of these people, including one where only a tomato is in focus. A 1962 photo shows one of these people in black suspenders with his hands held rigidly to his sides. Three of them were the subject of controversial photos by Sally Mann. Identical (*) twin people of this sort in black dresses appear in a photo from Roselle, New Jersey that was referenced by Stanley Kubrick in The Shining. Diane Arbus also depicted one of them holding a fake grenade in Central Park. Two of these people bury their faces behind a woman's back in a Dorothea Lange photo. For 10 points, identify this type of person, some of whom cling to the title woman in Migrant Mother.
2.r: children [or Sally Mann’s children; or kids; or preteens; or teenagers; accept any answer referring to people who are younger than adults]

2.q: In a photograph from this country, a man seems to bend impossibly backward in a curved, distorted brick corridor. A photographer from this country depicted themselves wearing a checkered shirt and glancing away from a mirror in a self-portrait. A photographer who worked in this country captured a woman resting her head on a table while clutching an African mask in her left hand in his Black and White. That photographer, who had an affair with Lee Miller, created (*) photograms with light-sensitive paper that he referred to as his namesake "-ographs." A photographer from this country depicted the stages of Pablo Picasso's work on Guernica. A photograph taken in this country displays two f-shaped violin holes painted on the back of the model Kiki. For 10 points, name this home country of Dora Maar and Claude Cahun.

In a picture by this photographer, a woman holding a parasol walks on the side of a dirt road as two men on motorcycles pass her. A bald woman holds her baby as a crowd of onlookers march in this photographer's The Shaved Woman of Chartres. This photographer's brother Cornell joined a cooperative he co-founded with Henri Cartier-Bresson and David Seymour, Magnum Photos. This photographer's collaborator Gerda Taro may have taken one of his images depicting Federico Borrell Garcia. While in French Indochina, this photographer (*) died after stepping on a landmine. The "Magnificent Eleven" images set on D-Day were captured by this photographer, who earlier depicted a loyalist militiaman losing his grip on his rifle after being shot during the Spanish Civil War. For 10 points, name this Hungarian war photographer who took The Falling Soldier.

In a photograph taken in this city, a man in the center jumps while a couple embraces to his right; that photo depicts the 100th anniversary of a landmark in this city. The Temple of Solomon was showcased in the first diorama theatre, which was built in this city. A dark, winding street serves as the cover image for a photography book depicting [this city] by Night. Henry Miller called the Hungarian artist (*) Brassai the "eye of" this city. The earliest known photograph of a person was taken in this city. A photograph taken in this capital city of a man leaping over a puddle was used to illustrate the concept of the "decisive moment." An artist used iodine crystals to develop an early photographic method in this capital city. For 10 points, in what capital city did Henri Cartier-Bresson and Louis Daguerre spend much of their careers working in?

Mabel Cramer and Miss Thompson were photographed in a series by this photographer and his collaborator Clarence Hudson White. This photographer depicted a carriage on a tree lined street in pouring rain titled Spring Showers, The Coach. This photographer photographed a famous sculpture placed in front of Marsden Hartley's The Warriors for the magazine The Blind Man. This photographer pioneered abstract photography in his series of clouds titled (*) Equivalents. This photographer of a lone smoking train also published the photographic journal Camera Work. One of this photographer's works depicts passengers traveling on the SS Kaiser Wilhelm. For 10 points, name this photographer of The Steerage who was married to Georgia O'Keeffe.

While living in this country, a photographer tinkered with lighting to capture soft-focus images, many of which feature children only wearing angel wings. A family surrounds a bedridden girl in a combination print of five images from this country titled Fading Away. A photographer from this non-France country founded a method of using silver iodide-coated paper to create blurry yet reproducible images called (*) calotypes. Photos of men of hero-worship from this country were taken by Julia Margaret Cameron. The first art institute to collect photographs is this country's V&A Museum. Many photographs of a monarch from this country show her wearing a small diamond crown. For 10 points, what country's Royal Photographic Society collection includes images of Queen Victoria?
2.r: the United Kingdom [accept British Empire or Great Britain; accept England]

2.q: A photographer from this country photographed a man pulling a row of toy horses in this country's capital. That photographer also captured two people kissing in front of a city hall. A photographer from this country photographed Alberto Giacometti walking while carrying one of his statues in his Walking Man series. This country's capital was depicted "by night" in a book by (*) Brassai. A photographer from this country photographed Mohandas Gandhi hours before his assassination. That photographer theorized the "decisive moment" and depicted a man leaping over a puddle of water in his Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare. For 10 points, identify this home country of Robert Doisneau and Henri Cartier-Bresson.

A photo named after this quality that features a woman sitting while holding her knee and tucking her head was subtitled "Charis ("kuh-riss"), Santa Monica" by its photographer, Edward Weston. A figure with this quality curls up against his wife, whose hair is spread out on a cream carpet, in an Annie Leibovitz photo of (*) John Lennon. A Winter 2014 cover of Paper magazine depicting its central figure looking back and pinching the sides of a shiny black dress was claimed to have "[broken] the internet" due to this quality of Kim Kardashian's back and butt. For 10 points, name this quality of wearing little to no clothing.
2.r: nudity [accept synonyms like nude or naked or unclothed; accept descriptions like not wearing clothing until mention; prompt on descriptions of being exposed or showing bare skin]

2.q: A woman in this painting with two white horns was copied for M. C. Escher's print Belvedere. In the bottom right corner of this painting, a pig wearing a nun's habit tries to kiss a naked man. Amelia Hamrick transcribed a "really bad Gregorian chant" from music written on a man's skin in this painting. When this painting is closed, it depicts a bare gray Earth surrounded by a cosmic sphere on the (*) third day of creation. Giant birds in this painting include a goldfinch holding grapes in a lake and a nightjar in a gold chair eating a man headfirst. This painting's right panel features giant musical instruments and a hollow "Tree-Man" as people are tortured in Hell. For 10 points, name this large triptych whose central panel depicts humans sinning in the title location, a painting by Hieronymus Bosch.

It's not Timothy, but an artist with this first name worked with Alexander Upshaw on the western images Canyon De Chelly and Old Eagle. Another artist with this first name depicted a nude Charis Wilson sitting on a blanket in Santa Monica. An artist with this first name was funded by J. P. Morgan to create the photobook The North American Indian and had the surname Curtis. Another artist with this first name pioneered adding color with layers of (*) gum bichromate print, and curated the MoMA exhibition The Family of Man. This is the first name of a Pictorialist who photographed the "still-lifes" Nautilus and Pepper No. 30, as well as another who created The Pond-Moonlight and The Flatiron. For 10 points, give this first name of photographers surnamed Weston and Steichen.
2.r: Edward [accept Edward Steichen or Edward Jean Steichen; accept Edward Weston or Edward Henry Weston; accept Edward S. Curtis or Edward Sheriff Curtis]

2.q: A series titled for these locations features a painting in which multiple shirtless men drag baskets across red ground. The artist of that series created two artworks depicting "masculine" and "feminine" versions of a subject in these locations. A large black animal in this location appears in a work titled for being set "off Goto" from a series of artworks titled for these locations "of Wisdom." In another series, an artwork depicting one of these locations is followed by a depiction of a bright (*) red mountain titled Fine Wind, Clear Morning. Import of Prussian blue from the Netherlands revolutionized Japanese depictions of these general locations, including a print in which Mount Fuji can be seen in the background of a scene set "off Kanagawa." For 10 points, in what general locations did Hokusai depict many fishers and whalers?
2.r: oceans [or seas or umi; accept One Thousand Pictures of the Ocean, One Thousand Pictures of the Sea, or Oceans of Wisdom; prompt on waves, Masculine Wave, Feminine Wave, or Great Wave off Kanagawa with “in what general location?”; prompt on bodies of water]

2.q: An artist from this country depicted a bird carving the back of a man with a knife while a woman sprouts from an egg in his painting Birds' Hell. That artist from this country depicted his wife Quappi in a pink jumper, and also painted soldiers hanging a man next to his bound and stripped wife in a crowded attic. In a triptych from this country, a woman with a pink ostrich feather in her hair dances as a legless soldier walks on crutches. An artist from this country painted a smoking man without a right (*) hand in his Self-Portrait As a Soldier. This country's art movements of New Objectivity and The Bridge were denounced by a regime that burned thousands of "degenerate" paintings. For 10 points, the artists Max Beckmann and Otto Dix were from what country that was ruled by the Nazi Party?
2.r: Germany [or Federal Republic of Germany or Bundesrepublik Deutschland] (The unnamed paintings in the second and third lines are The Night and Metropolis.)

2.q: A sculpture by Frederic Leighton responds to Laocoon and His Sons by depicting one of these people entwined with a python. An excavation at Akrotiri uncovered a fresco of these people featuring two boys wearing belts among the wall paintings of Thera. Because of its similar pose, the Esquiline Venus is sometimes considered a female version of a statue depicting one of these people. A sculpture of one of these people is imitated in the opening sequence of a Leni (*) Riefenstahl film subtitled Festival of Nations. That sculpture depicts one of these people in an unnatural pose, and is by Myron of Eleutherae. The Diadumenos depicts one of these people, who would have been common models for its sculptor Polykleitos. For 10 points, the Discophoros and Discobolus depict people of what profession as they would have competed in the Olympics?
2.r: athletes [accept wrestlers, discus-throwers, discus holders; boxers, or pugilists; accept olympians; accept Discophoros or Discobolus until read; accept Akrotiri Boxer Fresco; accept An Athlete Wrestling with a Python; prompt on diadem-bearers; prompt on Diadumenos until read]

2.q: In 2012, a Paris auction house unveiled a sheet containing fourteen sketches by this artist for a series of quickly executed genre portraits known as this artist's Fantasy Figures. In a painting by this artist, a child raises a stick with a rock hanging from it to the hand of a woman whose cheek is being tickled by a piece of straw. That painting is a metaphor for courtship and is a companion to this artist's erotically charged depiction of a girl on a (*) see-saw. This artist painted a layman instead of a bishop for a painting whose left side contains a depiction of Falconet's Menacing Love. This artist of Blind Man's Bluff and the "Progress of Love" series, painted a slipper flying off the foot of a woman as a reclining man looks up her pink dress. For 10 points, name this Rococo artist of The Swing.

Although this painting's artist wrote that "the ravages of the axe are daily increasing," the full title indicates that the broken trees in this painting were split by nature. Matthew Baigell notes that when viewed "from God's perspective," shapes in the background of this painting spell a Hebrew word. In this painting's foreground, a cross-shaped chair, a flag, and a portfolio with a signature sit above a small (*) self-portrait of the artist turning towards the viewer. This painting's peaceful setting may be based on one of its artist's earlier works for Luman Reed, The Pastoral State. This landscape painting is often read as an allegory for wilderness versus civilization due to a receding thunderstorm on the left. For 10 points, name this Hudson River School painting of the sharply winding Connecticut River by Thomas Cole.
2.r: The Oxbow [or View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm]

2.q: This artist painted Justice wielding a sword in a tondo above a painting by him in which a winged Gorgon head appears on a woman's chest. A study for a combat scene relief under a statue in one of this artist's paintings shows a nude man swinging a stick at another. In a painting by this artist, an altar holds an ostensory below four flying putti holding the gospels. Apollo plays a precursor to the modern violin while surrounded by poets and the (*) Muses on the title mountain in a painting by this artist. A man modeled on Bramante uses a compass in the bottom right of a painting by this artist housed in the Stanza della Segnatura with The Parnassus and La Disputa. This artist painted Plato pointing upward while talking to Aristotle among a group of philosophers. For 10 points, name this Renaissance artist of The School of Athens.
2.r: Raphael [or Raphael Sanzio da Urbino or Raffaelo Sanzio da Urbino]

2.q: Photos taken by a member of this group appeared in an exhibition subtitled "Eyes of the Storm." Richard Avedon modified pictures of this group by overlaying Day-Glo colors and symbols such as flowers and a dove. Harry Benson photographed this group posing with Muhammad Ali and having a pillow fight. The name of this group appears written in red flowers in front of a bass drum in a design by Jann Haworth and Peter Blake. This group hired Richard (*) Hamilton to create a minimalist design with a white background a year after they posed in front of 71 cardboard cutouts of celebrities. Iain Macmillan photographed this group walking on a zebra crossing to EMI studios for the cover of a project that opens with the track "Come Together." For 10 points, name this band depicted on the cover of their album Abbey Road.

This activity is depicted in the painting Summertime, as well as one its artist painted in Antibes ("ahn-TEEB") a year after the lost mural Modern Woman. The artist's brother-in-law Rodolphe Leenhoff does this activity behind a reclining woman in blue in a painting by Edouard Manet. In a painting titled for this activity, a man in black with a blue obi sash faces away from the viewer as a woman holds a pink-clad baby in her lap. The Phillips Collection houses a painting titled for this activity in which (*) Aline Charigot plays with a dog as Gustave Caillebotte ("KYE-butt") sits backward on a chair. In that painting titled for this activity, the artist's friends wear straw hats and talk under the striped awning of the Maison Fournaise restaurant. For 10 points, a luncheon takes place during a "party" of what activity in a painting by Pierre-Auguste Renoir?
2.r: boating [accept sailing or rowing; accept other descriptions of riding a boat; accept The Luncheon of the Boating Party or The Boating Party; prompt on partying or lunching until read with “What other activity titles that painting?”; prompt on sitting or feeding ducks with “While doing what other activity?”]

2.q: An early painting by this artist is titled The Ruins of Holyrood Chapel. A statue of Jupiter Tonans stands in front of drapery in a "still life" by this artist once housed at Kynzvart Castle. Another work by this artist depicts a man getting his shoes shined at the corner of a seemingly empty street. A feud between this artist of Boulevard du Temple and Henry Fox Talbot spawned after the latter introduced "salted paper" to one art form. This artist slowly phased out (*) bitumen use to improve one art form while working with Joseph Nicephore Niepce. In 1835, this artist invented a technique in which mercury fumes are exposed to an iodized silver-coated plate until an image appears. For 10 points, what Frenchman is the namesake of the first publicly available method of photography?

In his "Jpeg" series, an artist from this modern-day country appropriated overly-pixelated images of 9/11 found online. By projecting enlarged photos onto canvas, an artist from this country created blurry, photorealist paintings, such as one depicting two lit candles. Two artists from this country photographed many water towers in their grid-formatted typologies of industrial architecture. An artist in this country showed long convenience store shelves in (*) 99 Cent II Diptychon and edited buildings out for a wide, sparse photo of a river. A graffiti mural in this country by Dmitri Vrubel reproduces a photo of two world leaders sharing a fraternal kiss. For 10 points, name this country where the Bechers founded the School of Photography in Dusseldorf.
2.r: Federal Republic of Germany [or Bundesrepublik Deutschland] (The artists clued in the first four sentences are Thomas Ruff, Gerhard Richter, Bernd and Hilla Becher, and Andreas Gursky.)

2.q: A flower occludes the sweating face of an author from this country in an image taken for a photobook subtitled Killed by Roses. An artwork from this country depicting sheets of paper blown away into the sky serves as the basis for a staged photograph by Jeff Wall. An artist born in this country included the command, "let people copy or photograph your paintings," as an "event score" in an artist's book titled (*) Grapefruit. An artist born in this country is embraced by her nude husband in a 1980 photograph shot by Annie Leibovitz. That Fluxus artist from this country also permitted the audience to photograph her being dressed down by the public in the performance piece Cut Piece. For 10 points, what Asian country is the birthplace of Yoko Ono?
2.r: Japan [or Nippon-koku or Nihon-koku] (The author referenced in the first line is Yukio Mishima.)

2.q: Linda Gordon co-compiled images taken by this photographer into a photobook titled Impounded. In an image taken by this photographer, a billboard stating, "next time, try the train," juxtaposes two men walking. A trip taken by this photographer and Paul Taylor prompted the duo to capture an image of U.S. Route 54 and compile the photobook An American Exodus. It's not Ansel Adams, but this photographer captured a 1942 image of an American (*) flag flying in the middle of Manzanar while working as a correspondent for the War Relocation Authority. In an image taken by this photographer at Nipomo, California, two children hide their faces behind the shoulders of a pea picker named Florence Owens. For 10 points, name this Depression-era photographer of Migrant Mother.

3.q: A pro-Kremlin protester threw a jar of his urine at a photo of one of these people at a 2016 exhibition called Absence of Shame. The cover images of the collections The Last Day of Summer and Radiant Identities depict these people. Jock Sturges and David Hamilton have been criticized for their photographs of these people. These people are the subject of the photography book Tulsa by Larry Clark. In her early work, Sally Mann courted controversy with photographs of these people. Anne Geddes is best known for her photographs of these people. (*) Steve McCurry garnered fame for his photograph of one of these people in a red headscarf, which was displayed on the cover of National Geographic; that person of this type was from Afghanistan. For 10 points, name this type of person, one of whom was photographed holding a toy hand grenade in Central Park by Diane Arbus.
3.r: children [or young people; accept young girls or young boys; accept babies; accept teenagers; accept kids]
3.c: 2017 WAO Pkt Michigan + Maryland B Q13

3.q: Some members of this group, which included Henry Swift and Consuelo Kanaga first met at "683," a gallery on Brockhorst St. This group's first show was at the M. H. de Young Memorial Museum in San Francisco. Utilizing a technique one member of this group called "previsualization," which involved a flat plane of ground glass that reflected the scene, works like Dunes, Oceano and Succulent attempted to capture sharp-detail. This group's 1932 manifesto defines their work in contrast to the (*) "Pictorialist," which borrows principles from the graphic arts and painting as opposed to the pure or "straight" style of photography this group advocated. For 10 points identify this group formed by such figures as William Van Dyke, Edward Weston and Ansel Adams named after the smallest aperture of a large-format camera.
3.r: Group f/64

3.q: This photographer hid a 35mm Contax camera under his coat in order to discreetly take his "subway portraits." In this artist's photograph Penny Picture Display, hundreds of tiny portraits are overlaid by the word "STUDIO." This photographer befriended Ernest Hemingway when taking photographs for Carleton Beals's book The Crime of Cuba. Photographs by this man were reproduced and credited to another artist in a series titled After [this man] by the appropriation artist Sherrie Levine. A picture by this photographer depicts a thin-lipped (*) woman named Allie Mae Burroughs. While on leave from the Farm Security Administration, this man was commissioned by Fortune magazine to photograph tenant farmers in Alabama during the Great Depression. For 10 points, name this photographer who collaborated with writer James Agee on the book Let Us Now Praise Famous Men.
3.r: Walker Evans

3.q: Rebecca Solnit described how this place was captured using 18-by-22-inch glass "mammoth" plates by Carleton Watkins, who was one-upped by Eadweard Muybridge's "Flying Studio." A photograph of this location is part of a series of silver gelatin prints commissioned by Albert Bender with the made-up word "Parmelian" in its title. Judy Dater captured the photographer Imogen Cunningham stumbling upon a nude Twinka Thiebaud ("tee-BOH") at this location. This place was captured using a (*) deep-red filter to lower the exposure and create a jet black sky by a photographer standing at a perch called the "Diving Board." The Zone System was developed by a member of f/64 ("f-stop-64") who took High Trips to this location with the Sierra Club. For 10 points, Ansel Adams's photo Monolith depicts the Half Dome mountain of what National Park?
3.r: Yosemite National Park [anti-prompt on Half Dome by asking “what larger place is it in?”; prompt on the Sierra Nevadas or High Sierras by asking “what location in the Sierra Nevadas?”; prompt on the Wild West by asking “what specific location was the site of those photographs?”] (The Rebecca Solnit book is River of Shadows: Eadweard Muybridge and the Technological Wild West.)

3.q: This artist composed a Symphonic Set for Piano and Orchestra, which he premiered alongside conductor Dean Dixon in Venice. This composer of Martin documented the Causey family, who then were forced to leave town for their safety after the publication of "The Restraints: Open and Hidden." Before working at Life magazine, this person bought a camera from a pawnshop, learned how to use it, and worked for the FSA. This artist used a low angle to photograph a child who points at a white doll in (*) Doll Test. In one of this person's photographs, a man peers towards the right as he holds a manhole cover angled over his head. That photo by this man was part of a collaboration with Ralph Ellison for two largely unpublished essays and was titled The Invisible Man. For 10 points, name this artist who took a photo of a government cleaning woman called American Gothic, and who also directed the movie Shaft.
3.r: Gordon Parks
3.c: 2022 Chicago Open Pkt 04 Cheng + Coates + Bentley Q4

3.q: This artist appears as an elongated, spectral figure with his back to the moon in a black-and-white caricature by Marius de Zayas depicting him as the "midwife to ideas." This artist's tightly-framed depiction of a harnessed, castrated horse inspired a controversial nude portrait with the same name by Richard Prince depicting a 10-year-old Brooke Shields nude; that work is titled Spiritual America. This photographer fell out with his friend Charles Scheeler over a negative review criticizing his use of platinum paper, which he used in his portrait of (*) Marsden Hartley. Wheel trails in the snow lead the eye up to a dark horse pulling a carriage in one of his winter scenes, and in another, hot steam rises from a team of horses; those works are titled Winter, Fifth Avenue and The Terminal. He founded Gallery 291, whose "little galleries" launched the Photo-Secession. For 10 points, what American photographer married Georgia O'Keeffe?
3.r: Alfred Stieglitz

3.q: Unlike varieties used in other fields, varieties of these devices used in film-making typically have both weather-sealing and a long throw. Some of the fastest models of these devices are produced by Cosina Voigtlander. The entirety of John Ford's How the West Was Won was shot with two unusually shaped examples of these devices, one of which was also used in 2001: A Space Odyssey for shots from Hal's POV. To accommodate his camera moves, Steven Spielberg typically uses different wide varieties of these devices. Film crews on documentaries often use a (*) 70mm-200mm variety of these devices, while 28mm and 50mm primes are standard varieties of these devices. Unlike in photography, which mostly used fixed varieties as a primary one of these devices, most filmmakers instead use ones that allow for zoom. For ten parts, identify these devices, varieties of which like telephoto, anamorphic, and fisheye can produce very different levels of depth of field.
3.r: camera lens (accept specific kinds of lens like fisheye or telephoto lens)

3.q: This photographer worked in color more after completing a project on the topic of blue asbestos. A guitar hangs in the exact center of shelves of clothes in this artist's photograph Concession Store Interior. This artist was the only photographer to oppose using the camera "as a weapon" in the struggle for liberation at a 1982 Culture and Development Conference. One of this artist's photos depicts rows of bending workers' backs confined to the bottom third of the photo while brightly lit stone walls dominate the upper section. This artist's association with Optima magazine let him access the workplaces of the (*) Anglo-American corporation. Many collections by this man, such as The Transported of KwaNdebele, document apartheid. For 10 points, name this photographer who provided the visual components of the book On the Mines, a collaboration with Nadine Gordimer.
3.r: David Goldblatt

3.q: The documentary Shadow of the Iceberg debates the authenticity of a photo of Federico Borrell Garcia, who was this type of person. They are not soccer players, but these people are shown wading through water in the photographs known as "The Magnificent Eleven." Alexander Gardner and Tim (*) O'Sullivan are best known for taking photographs of these people in the 19th century. One of them is shown grasping his leg in Robert Capa's photograph entitled "The Falling" one of these. Robert F. Sargent showed these people moving towards a beach in his photo Into The Jaws of Death, while Joe Rosenthal showed several of them raising a flag at Iwo Jima. For 10 points, name this type of person whom Matthew Brady took pictures of during the Civil War.
3.r: soldiers [accept Spanish soldier before “The Magnificent Eleven”; prompt on anything relating to Spanish people before “The Magnificent Eleven”]

3.q: One work by this artist shows a bonnet-wearing woman carrying a butcher knife to the left of the artist's sister Katherine. Gertrude Kasebier and Clarence H. White joined an art movement led by this artist, which was created as a response to England's The Link Ring. Ten of his works called "Music" evolved into his series of abstract cloud depictions called (*) Equivalents. Horses pull a trolley labeled "Harlem" in his photograph The Terminal. In Camera Work, he frequently published the works of Edward Steichen, a man who co-founded New York's Gallery 291 with him. For 10 points, name this Photo-Secession photographer of The Steerage, the husband of Georgia O'Keeffe.
3.r: Alfred Stieglitz
3.c: 2014 SUBMIT Pkt 02. Illinois A, Alabama, Yale B Q1

3.q: Lynda Nead referred to the "double metamorphosis" of photographing one of these people in a discussion at the beginning of her book The Female Nude. A 1988 Annie Leibovitz photograph shows one of these people riding a white horse shirtless while smoking a cigar, and earlier she depicted him laying in a bed with Franco Columbu to promote a documentary. One of these people is shown sitting in profile on a throne naked while holding a cobra in Robert Mapplethorpe's 1983 collection Lady: Lisa Lyon. A burlesque woman with a (*) lampshade on her head appears next to one of these people who holds a large Tootsie Pop in Richard Hamilton's collage Just what is it that makes today's homes so different, so appealing? For 10 points, identify these athletes, the subjects of the 1977 documentary Pumping Iron which surrounds the rivalry between Lou Ferrigno and Arnold Schwarzenegger.
3.r: bodybuilders [accept clear knowledge equivalents; prompt on Lisa Lyon, Franco Columbu, or Arnold Schwarzenegger before mention]

3.q: Alberto Giacometti ("jacque"-a-metty) strides behind one of his Walking Man sculptures in an image by this artist. A man raises his hands while another looks on at a funeral pyre in one work by this artist, who showed the cremated man leaving a shrine alive just days earlier. This artist photographed some of the last imperial eunuchs in China, part of his series about "The Last Days of the Kuomintang." Henri Matisse designed the cover for a book by this artist which has a title that translates to (*) "images on the sly." This photographer, who took photos of India immediately after Gandhi's death, shot a man jumping over a ladder into a puddle in Behind Gare St. Lazare. For 10 points, identify this French photographer who developed the idea of capturing a "decisive moment."
3.r: Henri Cartier-Bresson

3.q: An image by this photographer depicting three men riding a canoe in Suzhou Creek is discussed in a 2015 essay by Teju Cole. This photographer claimed to have had an epiphany while viewing a Martin Munkacsi photograph of the backs of three naked children running into the surf of Lake Tanganyika. This photographer captured an image of people pushing against each other to buy gold from a bank during the Kuomintang's final days. In an image by this photographer, a staircase winds down next to a blurry (*) cyclist in motion. The name "RAILOWSKY" appears twice in the background of an image by this photographer depicting a man in the air having leapt off a ladder floating in a puddle. For 10 points, Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare is a work by what French photographer who sought to capture the "decisive moment?"
3.r: Henri Cartier-Bresson (The Teju Cole essay is “Perfect and Unrehearsed.”)
3.c: 2022 Penn Bowl Pkt Tiebreakers and Extras Q2

3.q: Skill at indoor self-portraits earned a photographer from this country the moniker "Queen of the Leica." A self-described professional voyeur from this country often posed alongside his wife, a photographer known as Alice Springs. Photographers from this country organized monochrome photographs of industrial environments into grids of "typologies." The mammoth photobook SUMO was published by a photographer from this country, where Lee Miller posed for a photo in a (*) bathtub. A photographer from this country edited out a dog walker from an image of a river between two green fields and captured a "diptych" in a supermarket. A mural in this country was inspired by a photograph of two male leaders kissing. For 10 points, Andreas Gursky studied at what country's School of Photography in Dusseldorf?
3.r: Germany [or Deutschland] (The photographers mentioned are, in order: Ilse Bing, Helmut Newton, and Hilla and Bernd Becher. The mural on the Berlin Wall depicts the fraternal kiss of Brezhnev and Honecker.)

3.q: Description acceptable. Felix de Weldon made a wax model of this image which he later used as the basis for a memorial he designed. Ira Hayes descended into alcoholism thanks to the fame given him by this "gung-ho" photograph, which was taken as its creator turned around, though for a half-century it was charged that this photograph was (*) staged. This photo taken by Joe Rosenthal depicts six men, only three of whom lived through the year, on top of Mount Suribachi. For 10 points, name this iconic WWII photo showing a flag being raised during a Pacific battle.
3.r: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima [accept anything involving a flag and Iwo Jima]

3.q: This noun partly titles a book by Geoff Dyer that claims William Eggleston's photos look like they were taken by a Martian who ended up in Memphis. An exhibition titled for this noun was divided into "X," "Y," and "Z" portfolios and had its premiere at D.C.'s Corcoran Gallery canceled. This noun appears in the English title of a book whose cover features Henri Matisse cutouts of vegetative forms, and which includes an image of boys playing near a bombed-out wall. This noun is modified by (*) "perfect" in the title of a 1989 retrospective on Robert Mapplethorpe. A concept named for this noun is illustrated by photos of a cyclist taken from atop a staircase and a man jumping into a puddle behind the Gare Saint-Lazare ("garr san la-ZARR"), and refers to the ideal time to capture a photo. For 10 points, Henri Cartier-Bresson sought to photograph the "decisive" form of what period of time?
3.r: moment [accept The Ongoing Moment or The Perfect Moment or The Decisive Moment]

3.q: This woman's face is superimposed over rock formations five times in a photo by Richard Avedon, who shot a highly overexposed close-up of her face for a poster. Louis Vuitton designed his smaller Speedy 25 handbag for this woman, who also wore the specially-made perfume L'Interdit ("lan-tair-DEE"). This woman donned Oliver Goldsmith's oversized Manhattan sunglasses with Roger Scemama's ("seh-MA-ma's") layered pearl necklace for a film role in which she uses a foot-long (*) cigarette holder. As part of Hubert de Givenchy's ("yoo-BAIR duh zhee-von-SHEE's") close collaboration with this woman, she wore opera gloves and his iconic "little black dress" for a 1961 film that opens with her visiting the title luxury jewelry store in New York City. For 10 points, name this fashion icon and star of the films Funny Face and Roman Holiday, who played Holly Golightly in Breakfast at Tiffany's.
3.r: Audrey Hepburn [reject “Katharine Hepburn”] (The first sentence describes a poster for the film Funny Face, whose protagonist was based on Avedon.)

3.q: This man once advertised for subjects in the newspaper with the line "you cannot tell how soon it may be too late." The New York Times wrote that this man has "laid" his subjects "in our dooryards and along the streets" in works created in "what-is-it wagons." This student of William Page took a picture of an actor in the same setting dressed as Spartacus, Richard III, and himself; that actor was Edwin Forrest. This man had Francis d'Avignon create a book of lithographs based on his work, including portraits of William Channing and (*) Millard Fillmore. This creator of the Gallery of Illustrious Americans employed Timothy O'Sullivan and Alexander Gardner to create works like one showing a mass of bodies lying next to a fence. For 10 points, name this Civil War photographer of "The Dead at Antietam."
3.r: Mathew Brady

3.q: For one shot, this artist was only permitted to use three flashbulbs, but lost one to the heat and moisture and forgot to pull the slide on another, leaving only one flash usable. Aerial photographs by this artist include one in which a DC-4 flies over Manhattan. Though not Annie Leibovitz, this artist is shown seated on one of the sculpted eagles of the Chrysler Building in another photo. This artist took a shot of Montana's Fort Peck Dam which appeared on the first cover of (*) LIFE magazine following its 1936 relaunch. Together with her onetime husband Erskine Caldwell, she documented the lives of sharecroppers in the Deep South in the book You Have Seen Their Faces. She was the first female photographer to cover World War II. For 10 points, name this American photojournalist who photographed Mahatma Gandhi at his spinning wheel.
3.r: Margaret Bourke-White

3.q: One of these animals is depicted in a photograph titled for an "Imaginary" figure associated with them by an artist dubbed "the Norwegian Cindy Sherman," Anja Niemi. Turner Prize-winner Mark Wallinger bought one of these animals and named it A Real Work of Art as a readymade sculpture. A photographer borrowed the title of an earlier photograph of this animal to name a re-photographing of a Gary Gross picture depicting ten-year-old Brooke Shields in a bathtub. That original photograph of one of these animals is (*) Spiritual America by Alfred Stieglitz. A cigarette advertisement depicting one of these animals by Sam Abell was re-photographed by Richard Prince. The inventor of the zoopraxiscope created one of the first moving image sequences by capturing one of these animals named Sallie Gardner. That sequence by Edweard Muybridge depicts this animal "in Motion." For 10 points, name this animal that appears in the photo Untitled (Cowboy).
3.r: horses

3.q: Thomas Struth ("shtroot") photographed a group of schoolgirls at this museum sketching a painting from its collection. In 2015, this museum created 3D copies of six of its pieces, including The Nobleman with a Hand on His Chest, for an exhibit for the blind titled "Touching [this museum]." Its first solo exhibition of a female artist was a 2016 showing of the seventeenth-century painter Clara Peeters. In 2009, it partnered with Google Earth to produce fourteen-thousand-megapixel digitizations of pieces like Rubens's The Three Graces. The Baron d'Erlanger ("bah-ROHN dair-lon-ZHAY") donated a series of paintings to this museum. After Picasso's Guernica left the MoMA, it was housed here until it was transferred in 1991 to a nearby museum next to the (*) Thyssen-Bornemisza ("TEE-same-bor-nay-MEE-sah") Museum. In 1879, John Singer Sargent visited this museum and copied one of its paintings in preparation for painting The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit. This museum houses Van der Weyden's ("VY-dun's") Deposition and Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights. For 10 points, name this museum home to Goya's Black Paintings and Velazquez's Las Meninas, located in Madrid.
3.r: Museo del Prado [or the Prado; prompt on Casón del Buen Retiro]

3.q: After his wife passed, a photographer from this country took many melancholy still-lifes of glass ornaments and vases with an SX-70 gifted to him by Polaroid. A photographer born in this country took many surreal nudes in 1933's Distortion series, as well as The Fork and Mondrian's Glasses and Pipe. That photographer's nighttime photos of the Seine ("sen") inspired a younger street photographer born in this country who was nicknamed the "eye of Paris" by his friend, Henry (*) Miller. That photographer captured a cobblestone road gleaming with rain for the cover of his book Paris By Night. A photographer [emphasize] born in this country who was killed in French Indochina captured the D-Day landings in The Magnificent Eleven and a Republican soldier being shot in The Falling Soldier. For 10 points, name this home country of Brassai ("brah-sah-EE"), Andre Kertesz ("KEHR-tayss"), and Robert Capa.
3.r: Hungary [or Magyarország]
3.c: 2023 Chicago Open Pkt 06 - McCullar et al, Du et al Q18

3.q: Hundreds of this artist's answering machine tapes were acquired by Chris McKim for a 2020 documentary that features numerous interviews with Fran Lebowitz. This artist was awarded one dollar in damages after suing the American Family Association for using his work out of context. A film by this artist and Richard Kern was based on an incident where this artist's father force-fed him his pet rabbit. The Smithsonian censored eleven seconds of a video work by this artist in which (*) ants crawl over a crucifix. A recent retrospective of this artist at the Whitney titled History Keeps Me Awake at Night featured several photos of him by Peter Hujar. This artist created an untitled photograph depicting buffaloes falling off a cliff that was used as cover art on U2's single "One." For 10 points, name this New York photographer of A Fire in My Belly who died of AIDS in 1992.
3.r: David Wojnarowicz (“voy-nuh-ROH-vitch”) [or David Michael Wojnarowicz]

3.q: This period inspired a "diary" of five photographs whose "14.00 ("fourteen hundred") hours" entry depicts its artist standing dramatically in an ornate study, clutching a bundle of papers in his non-paralyzed hand. A photographer active during this period spliced together images of a "venerable" sage and a veiled nude to form the center of his photomontage The Two Ways of Life. John the Baptist's severed head rests serenely in a bowl in one of this period's popular "headless portraits" captured by Oscar (*) Rejlander ("ray-LAHN-dehr"). J. J. Mayall captured 14 cartes de visite of this period's namesake, who amassed a collection of photographs by Henry Fox Talbot. A photographer active during this era captured Arthurian-inspired portraits in her characteristic soft-focus style to illustrate a contemporary's Idylls of the King. For 10 points, Julia Margaret Cameron was active during what regnal era?
3.r: Victorian era [prompt on the 19th century or 1800s] (The lead-in is Yinka Shonibare’s Diary of a Victorian Dandy.)

3.q: A photographer from this country depicted a nude young couple clad in raincoats, sitting in the trees at different elevations, in a photograph often compared to depictions of Adam and Eve. That photographer from this country took a picture of a musician with dyed green hair in Frank, in the shower, which became the cover to Frank Ocean's Blonde. Another photographer from this country digitally edited a power station out of a huge (*) color photograph depicting a river, and captured a dizzyingly well-stocked supermarket in his photo 99 Cent. Monkeys take over a raft as the title conquistador vows to establish a dynasty in a film from this country, Aguirre ("uh-GHEE-ruh"), the Wrath of God. For 10 points, name this home country of Wolfgang Tillmans, Andreas Gursky and Werner Herzog.
3.r: Germany [or Federal Republic of Germany; accept Deutschland; accept West Germany]

3.q: A character who is named in reference to this person in the credits of a film is a motorcycle-riding TMZ paparazzo with a reflective helmet. Thom Andersen's 1975 documentary about this person includes a recreation of this person's depiction of two women kissing. Early in Nope, OJ Haywood shows a clip of this person's work and claims to be a direct (*) descendant of the man depicted in the clip. The film pioneer Etienne-Jules Marey ("et-yen zhool mah-REH") was influenced by this person's work in Palo Alto under the patronage of Leland Stanford. This person depicted Sallie Gardner in what is often considered one of the first motion pictures in history. For 10 points, The Horse in Motion was one of the pioneering studies of motion by what English photographer?
3.r: Eadweard Muybridge [or Edward James Muggeridge; accept Eadweard Muybridge, Zoopraxographer]
3.c: 2023 On Cinema at the Buzzer Pkt 07 Q2

3.q: In one photograph taken in this city, a man gets his shoes shined on a foot rest advertising Cherry Blossom Light Tan Shoe Polish in front of a cinema showing the film Rocky 2 . It's not Paris, but in this city, photographs of fish workers and a shot of a man sleeping on newspapers below a crowd of spectators to a 1937 event were taken by Henri Cartier-Bresson. Before his series of nudes, a photograph series titled "Camera in" this city was made by Bill Brandt. In this city, (*) Iain MacMillan took a photo of men dressed in, from left to right, blue, grey, black and white. Rumours of one man's death read significance into a 1969 photo taken in this city for which a local policeman had to briefiy close the title street. For 10 points, name this city where four musicians were photographed crossing a zebra crossing for the cover of the album Abbey Road .
3.r: London [or City of Westminster ] (The first photo is by William Klein and is titled ‘Shoes Polisher, Rocky II, etc, Piccadilly’)

3.q: A photograph taken in this country shows a group of women and children grasping onto each other while navigating a canal. Larry Wayne Chaffin slightly smiles while wearing a headband message in a photo taken in this country by Horst Faas. Photographer Dickey Chapelle was depicted receiving last rights in this country by fellow photographer Henri Huet. In this country, photographer Art Greenspon captured (*) Watson Baldwin raising his hands in the air. Nick Ut spent the 50th anniversary of a photograph of this country with its subject, who fled a burning village while naked and crying. "The Terror of War" was taken in this country, in which Eddie Adams photographed the moment an officer is summarily executed. For 10 points, name this country, the subject of the war photograph "Saigon Execution."
3.r: Vietnam [or Socialist Republic of Vietnam; or North Vietnam; or South Vietnam; or the Democratic Republic of Vietnam; accept Vietnam War]

3.q: This artist's brother posed for portraits as Pierrot "laughing" and "running." Twelve profiles of this artist and this artist's brother Adrien were displayed in sequence to create two "revolving portraits." Claude Monet used this artist's studio at No. 35 to paint the Boulevard des Capucines and to exhibit Impression, Sunrise. A stunt by this artist inspired the Belgian term for crowd-control barriers. Caricatures of many of this artist's colleagues appear in giant lithographs that this artist termed his (*) "Pantheon." This artist wired together Bunsen "batteries" as artificial lights to photograph the Paris catacombs. This artist's top hat flies away in an Honore Daumier cartoon that depicts him "elevating Photography to Art." For 10 points, name this French photographer who used a hot air balloon to take aerial photographs of Paris and went by a one-word pseudonym.
3.r: Nadar [or Gaspard-Félix Tournachon]

3.q: A photo of this location makes up the cover of an early DIY catalog with the slogan "Access to Tools." A 2013 day about smiling was centered on a composite photo titled after this location. Due to his access to color processing, Raul Rodriguez developed a 95-degree rotated photo showing this location at the center taken using a heavily modified Hasselblad Camera. William Anders captured that photo partially named after this location, described by Galen Rowell as "the most influential (*) environmental photograph" ever. A photo in the "Family Portrait" series shows faint bands of light cutting across this object which takes up less than a pixel in it. The Sun half illuminates this object in a lunar-orbit photo showing its "rise." For 10 points, name this object, the center of the "Pale Blue Dot" and "Blue Marble" photos.
3.r: Earth [accept Earthrise; accept the globe; accept Terra, accept pale blue dot before read]

3.q: Berenice Abbot worked as an assistant to this photographer, who, like her, championed the empty street views of Eugene Atget ("aht-JAY"). This photographer captured another artist nude with ink over her palm and forearm, standing behind a printing wheel. With their lover, this photographer developed a technique of exposing a developing image to a flash of light called solarisation. The torso of that lover, Lee Miller, appears in one of this photographer's (*) namesake photograms. A woman rests her head next to an upright African mask in this photographer's Noir et blanche, and his portrait of an artist wearing a hat and pearls is the label of the Belle Haleine ("HA-lene") perfume bottle. In a photo by this man, Kiki de Montparnasse's nude back has two f-holes painted on it. For 10 points, Le Violon d'Ingres was taken by what Surrealist?
3.r: Man Ray (The powerbreak clue refers to a rayograph.)

3.q: Either a real name or a description like "the dwarf from Las Meninas" is acceptable. In one photo, this person is shown in profile sitting with three small children on the left side of the frame while the right side shows their adopted daughter in a mirror looking at a framed photo of this person's parents. The most famous image of this person was deliberately taken in an office belonging to a woman with a desk job that this person was passed over for. This person and their children and grandchildren appeared in a 60-photo series created by a photographer who later documented (*) Jim Crow Alabama in the Life series The Restraints: Open and Hidden. In a 1942 photograph, this person wears a polka-dotted dress and round glasses while holding a broom and mop in front of an American flag. For 10 points, name this government worker who appears in a Gordon Parks photograph titled for a Grant Wood painting.
3.r: Ella Watson [or the charwoman from American Gothic; accept cleaning woman or cleaning lady or janitor or custodian from American Gothic]

3.q: A photograph taken in this city shows three people dressed in yellow standing on the sidewalk staring intently to the left of the frame. John Maloof found thousands of photographs taken on a Rolleiflex ("ROH-lif-lex") in a storage unit in this city taken by the nanny of the Gensburg family, inspiring a documentary titled for "Finding" that woman who mostly lived here. Over 150,000 street photos were taken by (*) Vivian Maier in this city. In this city, Nathan Lerner discovered janitor Henry Darger's mixed-media outsider art narrative about the Vivian Girls. A sculpture inspired by liquid mercury is a common photo backdrop in this city's Millenium Park. For 10 points, name this city where many tourists take photos with Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate, a sculpture nicknamed "The Bean."
3.r: Chicago

3.q: In a series of photographic negatives from this country, 10 naked artists formed a pile to add one metre of height to a mountain. An artist's face is gradually covered with his relatives' names in another series of photographs from this country. That artist from this country photographed himself covered in honey, fish oil, and flies in the piece12 Square Metres. Photographs of an event in this country were hidden inside a toilet and smuggled out in a box of (*) tea. Jeff Widener's photographs of this country include a portrait of a Goddess of Democracy, and one where an unidentified man holding 2 shopping bags stands in front of a line of Type 59 Tanks. For 10 points, Tank Man was photographed in which country, where Zhang Huan ("jang h'wahn") worked with the Beijing East Village Collective?
3.r: China [or Zhōngguó; accept People's Republic of China; accept Zhōnghuá Rénmín Gònghéguó; accept PRC; do NOT accept or prompt on “Republic of China” or “ROC”]

3.q: At age 14, Stephen Shore cold-called this photographer and sold three photos to begin his career. This avid horticulturist took the photo Heavy Roses and exhibited many new breeds of delphinium. This photographer likened an actress to a leopardess behind shrubbery in a photo of her face with a piece of black lace suspended in front of it. This photographer won an Oscar for directing the World War II documentary The (*) Fighting Lady. Inspired by both Whistler's Nocturnes and an earlier photo of the same subject, this photographer used gum bichromate in his image of the Flatiron Building. This native Luxembourger shot The Pond-Moonlight and chose 503 photos from 68 countries for a 1955 event at the MoMA. For 10 points, Alfred Stieglitz co-founded the Photo-Secessionist gallery 291 with what curator of the exhibition The Family of Man?
3.r: Edward Steichen [or Éduard Jean Steichen] (The actress in the third sentence is Gloria Swanson.)

3.q: A photographer from this country depicted a reclining woman on a checkered blanket who is often called an odalisque. Like Brassai in France, a photographer from this country was dubbed the "Eye of" its capital for 1960s scenes of its swinging nightlife, such as one of a couple dancing on Christmas Eve. Ritual artworks from this country called boli feature in a film in which a man flees his father with stolen fetishes. World Heritage Sites in this country include a stepped pyramidal (*) tomb with sticks jutting out and a building from which palm bundles called toron stick out. The film Yeelen is from this country, where a Sudano-Sahelian building originally from the 13th century is the largest mud brick structure in the world. For 10 points, name this home country of the Tomb of Askia Mohammad and the Great Mosque of Djenne.
3.r: Mali [or Republic of Mali; or Republik bu Maali; or Jumhūriyyet Māli] (The photographers in the first two sentences are, respectively, Seydou Keïta and Malick Sidibé.)
